editorial:
Ever heard someone say they aren't racist, but then follow it up with something totally biased? You will see that exact awkwardness play out in this bold documentary. It follows Stacey Morrison and Tāmati Rimene-Sproat as they dive deep into the hidden prejudices in Aotearoa. Instead of just lecturing the audience, they use funny social experiments and real-life talks to show how bias works in the real world. The vibe is a mix of a serious classroom discussion and a casual chat with friends, making a heavy topic feel way more approachable and less like a textbook.

What really makes this work is the chemistry between the hosts; they keep the energy high so you never feel bored. The pacing is snappy, though some of the experiments might feel a bit repetitive if you aren't fully invested. You should definitely watch this if you want to understand people better or just want to challenge your own thinking. To get the best experience, try streaming it in 4K Ultra HD on Prime Video for those crisp visuals, or you can rent it on Apple TV for a quick movie night with the family.
endingExplained: The movie wraps up by bringing all the experiment participants back together for a final talk. They realize that everyone has some level of bias, no matter how hard they deny it. The final scenes show the hosts emphasizing that admitting your faults is the only way to actually change. It ends on a hopeful note, suggesting that open honesty and laughter can break down the walls of racism in New Zealand.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves social experiments and learning about human behavior.
